summaries.example: Imagine translating a funny story from another language. You would not replace every word mechanically. You would try to keep the story’s feeling, humor, and meaning while making it understandable to your readers. Schlegel thought good translators faced this kind of challenge.
summaries.summary: August Wilhelm von Schlegel was an important figure in German Romanticism, a movement that supported imagination, feeling, history, and creative art. He helped edit the journal Athenaeum with his brother Friedrich and gave lectures about literature and art. These lectures helped Romantic ideas travel across Europe. Schlegel was especially famous for translating Shakespeare into German, and he also translated works from Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Sanskrit, and other languages. He believed that a translation should carry the spirit of a work, not just replace each word. In his thinking about art, he disagreed with the idea that art is simply a copy of nature. Nature, for him, was a creative and changing power, and great art should create a complete world of its own. He also said that language is creative, rhythmic, and connected to poetry. A critic, in his view, should teach people how to understand art in its historical and cultural setting. Schlegel admired many different traditions, although his support for German culture sometimes existed alongside his wish for a world-spanning, cosmopolitan culture. The entry presents him as a thinker who made difference itself important: ancient and modern art, different languages, and different cultures could each have their own kind of greatness.
key_ideas: August Wilhelm von Schlegel was a German writer, teacher, translator, poet, and scholar.
He helped develop and spread German Romanticism across Europe, especially through journals, lectures, and translations.
He believed art does more than copy nature: it creates an organized, living world of its own.
He thought language is creative and musical, not merely a set of labels for objects.
He studied different cultures and languages and helped establish Sanskrit studies in Germany.
He valued differences among works of art and cultures instead of judging everything by one standard.
summaries.why_it_matters: Schlegel’s work shows how studying art can connect history, language, culture, and philosophy. His translations helped readers encounter famous works from other places. His ideas also encourage us to ask whether art must copy reality and whether one artistic standard should judge every culture. His life reminds us that a person can value both international exchange and a strong connection to a home culture, even when those commitments create tension.

important_terms.definition: A European cultural movement that valued imagination, feeling, history, creativity, and new ways of making art.
Careful study and judgment of art or writing. A critic tries to help people understand why a work matters.
Changing words or writing from one language into another while trying to preserve meaning and effect.
A way of making art that copies the outside appearance of nature as closely as possible.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between copying something and creating something inspired by it?
Why might a translator need to think about feelings and rhythm, not only individual words?
Can two very different kinds of art both be excellent? Why?
How could learning about another culture change the way someone understands its art?

summaries.example: Suppose a translator is working on a Shakespeare play. A word-for-word version may preserve dictionary meanings but lose the play’s rhythm, humor, dramatic force, or cultural distance. Schlegel’s approach asks the translator to study the original closely while recreating its artistic effect in the new language. The result should not become an awkward imitation of the source, but neither should it erase the source’s otherness.
summaries.summary: August Wilhelm von Schlegel was a German critic, translator, lecturer, poet, and scholar who played a major role in the formation and international circulation of early German Romanticism. With Friedrich Schlegel, he edited Athenaeum, a periodical that created space for experimental forms and new approaches to literature. His lectures in Jena, Berlin, and Vienna organized Romantic ideas into a broad history of European art and literature; the Vienna lectures in particular circulated widely through translation. Schlegel’s aesthetics rejects a simple version of the classical doctrine that art imitates nature. He distinguishes nature understood as fixed physical objects from nature understood philosophically as an organic, productive process. Art imitates nature in the second sense: a successful work generates an internally coherent world and expresses a search for unity. Romantic modernity, however, is marked by a consciousness of division between the human subject and the world, or between the finite and the infinite. Art therefore embodies longing for reconciliation rather than possessing absolute beauty itself. Schlegel’s account of criticism joins philosophical interpretation to historical and cultural knowledge. A critic should not impose personal or provincial preferences, but should learn how a work’s conditions shape its form. His account of language likewise resists a choice between emotional sound and rational convention: both belong to language, whose rhythm and metaphor make it creative. This view supports his practice as a translator of Shakespeare, Calderón, Italian, Portuguese, and Sanskrit works. key_ideas: Schlegel helped turn Romanticism into an organized intellectual and cultural movement through Athenaeum, his lectures, and his critical writing.
His lectures presented European literature and art historically, arguing that ancient and modern forms should be understood on their own terms rather than ranked by a single model.
He reinterpreted the claim that art imitates nature: because nature is an ongoing creative process, art imitates nature by producing an organic whole, not by making a photographic copy.
Romantic art expresses longing for a unity between finite human experience and a larger or infinite whole, while recognizing that the division cannot simply be erased.
Schlegel treats language as both conventional and expressive. It is a system of communication, but also rhythmic, emotional, metaphorical, and world-shaping.

His theory of translation combines fidelity to the original with adaptation to the receiving language; the translator must preserve meaning without making the foreign text either incomprehensible or falsely familiar.
summaries.why_it_matters: Schlegel matters because he helped establish influential ways of thinking about modern art, literary history, translation, and cultural comparison. His work challenges the assumption that criticism is only personal taste or that translation is mechanical substitution. It also offers a model of criticism that combines theory with close attention to particular works. At the same time, the entry does not present his ideas as free of tension: his openness to other cultures and ideal of cosmopolitan exchange existed alongside claims about German cultural centrality and national identity. important_terms.definition: The late-eighteenth- and early-nineteenth-century movement Schlegel helped shape, emphasizing imagination, history, feeling, creativity, and the significance of modern art.
The philosophical and critical study of art, including questions about beauty, artistic creation, historical forms, and aesthetic experience.
The view that art is primarily a copy or representation of nature’s visible forms; Schlegel criticizes this when nature is treated as a fixed object.
Schlegel’s term for the creative, unifying quality that makes an artwork more than a collection of techniques or parts.
A translator’s effort to preserve a work’s artistic spirit and cultural character rather than merely substituting words.
A critical approach that compares works across periods, cultures, and languages while attending to their differences.
A commitment to cultural exchange and a perspective wider than one nation, which in Schlegel sometimes coexisted uneasily with German cultural nationalism.
A belief that a work’s excellence can arise from an unconscious as well as conscious creative process, rather than from deliberate rule-following alone.

questions_to_think_about: If art creates its own world, what should count as success: resemblance to reality, internal unity, emotional power, or something else?
Does recognizing historical and cultural difference make criticism more fair, or can it make shared standards harder to defend?
Can a translation preserve a work’s spirit without changing it significantly?
How might language both describe the world and help construct the world we experience?
What does Schlegel’s mixture of cosmopolitanism and nationalism reveal about the limits of his critical ideal?

summaries.example: Consider a student translating a song for a school performance. Replacing every word exactly may produce awkward lines and lose the song’s mood. But changing everything to fit local slang may hide where the song came from. Schlegel’s view suggests balancing both goals: understand the original carefully, then create a natural version that keeps its energy and important differences.
summaries.summary: August Wilhelm von Schlegel was a German writer whose work connected literary criticism, philosophy, translation, language study, and cultural history. He became one of the central figures in early German Romanticism. Together with his brother Friedrich, he edited Athenaeum, a journal that welcomed essays, fragments, letters, dialogues, and different opinions while promoting new ideas about art. Schlegel also gave lectures in Jena, Berlin, and Vienna. These lectures explained the history of European literature and helped Romantic ideas spread beyond Germany. He was a highly successful translator, especially known for his German versions of Shakespeare, but he also worked with Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Latin, and Sanskrit materials. Schlegel disagreed with a simple picture of art as a mirror that copies nature. He understood nature as a living, productive process. Therefore, art imitates nature by creating an organic whole with its own unity. Romantic art also expresses longing for a lost or unreachable unity between the self and the universe. Ancient art, in his account, is more closely connected with present enjoyment and harmony, while modern art is more reflective, divided, and oriented toward desire. His theory of language combines two positions that might seem opposed: language expresses feeling through sound and rhythm, but it also depends on shared conventions and signs. Because language helps shape how people understand the world, it is creative as well as communicative. Schlegel’s approach to criticism asks readers to respect differences among cultures, periods, and artistic forms. key_ideas: Schlegel helped create and explain early German Romanticism, especially through Athenaeum and his public lectures.
He argued that modern and ancient art should not be judged as if one were simply a failed version of the other.
For him, nature was an active, creative whole, so art imitates nature by creating an organized world rather than copying appearances.
He saw Romantic art as expressing a desire to overcome a deep split between people and the wider universe, even though that split cannot be completely removed.
He treated language as both a system of shared signs and a living, rhythmic expression of feeling and imagination.
His translations and studies brought Shakespeare, Sanskrit, and other traditions to wider audiences, helping the growth of comparative literary study.
summaries.why_it_matters: Schlegel’s ideas matter because they changed how many readers thought about modern literature and about relations between cultures. He helped make Shakespeare more widely known in German-speaking Europe and helped spread Romantic theories through lectures and translation. His work also supports a careful kind of comparison: instead of asking whether every work follows one model, we can ask what kind of unity, purpose, and historical meaning it has. His mixed attitudes toward international culture and national identity give students a useful example of how a thinker’s ideas may contain both broad openness and serious limits.

important_terms.definition: A movement in European culture that emphasized imagination, emotion, history, creativity, and the special character of modern art.
The study and evaluation of art or literature, often using historical knowledge to explain how a work creates its effects.
The process of expressing a work in another language while trying to preserve its meaning, tone, and artistic character.
The belief that art mainly copies nature or the visible world. Schlegel challenged this narrow understanding.
A feeling of reaching toward a unity or ideal that seems absent or difficult to recover, an important feature of Romantic art.
The study of literature across languages, nations, and periods, with attention to both connections and differences.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a critic need to know a work’s history and culture before judging it?
Is a modern play unfairly judged if people compare it only with ancient rules?
What can rhythm or tone communicate that dictionary meanings cannot?
When does sharing a national culture support understanding, and when might it become narrow or exclusionary?
Why could preserving a foreign work’s differences be important in translation?
